title: We die daily
hook: each day a little of life is taken from us (Letters 24)

segments.voice: Yesterday: real joy, the serious kind. Your line was learn how to feel joy. Did you find a hearth, not a sparkler? Day four hundred fifty-four.
screen: `REAL JOY — LEARN HOW TO FEEL JOY.`

segments.voice: Lucilius is anxious. An enemy is threatening him with a lawsuit, and he has written to Seneca about how it might turn out. The twenty-fourth letter talks him through the fear. Then, near the end, Seneca reaches for a simple object: the clepsydra, a water clock, a vessel that marks time as the water runs out of it. And he turns it on the whole of a life. Today: we die daily.
screen: `AN ENEMY THREATENS A LAWSUIT.` → `SENECA TALKS HIM THROUGH IT.` → `THE WATER CLOCK, TURNED ON A LIFE.`

segments.voice: First, the line. In Latin, cotidie morimur: we die every day. Seneca explains it at once. Every day, some part of life is taken away. Even while we're growing up, life is shrinking. We lost childhood, then youth, and every yesterday up to this one. This very day we're dividing with death. Second, the water clock. It isn't the last drop that empties the clepsydra, he says, but everything that flowed out before it. The final hour doesn't make death. It only finishes it. Death has been arriving slowly all along. Third, why say something this bleak to a frightened friend? Because it shrinks the fear. If dying is something we've been doing every day, quietly, the last day is less of a monster. It's the end of a long and ordinary process, not an ambush. Seneca also warns against the opposite mistake: some people grow so tired of living that they long for death. He wants neither terror nor weariness, just clear sight. Fourth, what it does to today. If this day is being spent whether you notice or not, the question isn't whether to spend it. It's how. That's the same thread as the first letter, hold every hour, now seen from the other side. Not a reason for gloom. A reason to look up from the screen and notice the water running.
screen: `COTIDIE MORIMUR: WE DIE EVERY DAY.` · `NOT THE LAST DROP EMPTIES THE CLOCK.` · `NEITHER TERROR NOR WEARINESS.` · `TODAY IS BEING SPENT. HOW?` · then, large: `WE DIE DAILY.`

segments.voice: Sit still and listen to whatever is ticking: a clock, your heartbeat, your breath going in and out. Each breath is one drop from the vessel. Not frightening, just true. Let a few of them pass, and simply count them going. Then ask, gently: what is this morning, this afternoon, this evening being spent on? No judgment. Just notice where the water is going. The bell holds the time.
We die daily. Seneca's cotidie morimur: every day a little of life is spent, so the last hour only finishes what has been happening all along. Today's word.
Your line: we die daily. Once today, at a stoplight or a kettle, notice that this hour is being spent. Then spend the next few minutes on purpose. Day four hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners pause during the day to remember that time is passing, and use that reminder to choose what the next hour is for.

fork.setup: you're Seneca, and your friend is losing sleep over a lawsuit. what do you write?
options: think it through calmly, and remember we've been dying a little every day.
fork.reveal: Seneca walks Lucilius through the fear, then reminds him dying is a daily process, which shrinks the terror of any single day.

original.note: Latin, Seneca, Letters 24.20: we die every day.

trapdoor: what you thought: we die daily is a gloomy thing to say.
what it means: each day spends a little life, so the last day is no ambush, and today deserves care.
what a scholar hears: Letters 24.20 uses the clepsydra image; the same letter (24.22–25) warns against libido moriendi, a longing for death.
